title: Record Danube lows force Hungary's only nuclear plant offline as heatwave peaks
dek: Hungary's Paks nuclear power plant is shutting down entirely for the first time because the Danube's water level has fallen so low its cooling system cannot function. The closure coincides with a heatwave pushing temperatures to 37 degrees Celsius and comes as Serbia and Romania face identical water scarcity crises.
author: The GoCheckMyNews Desk
key_fact: Paks, which supplies a significant portion of Hungary's electricity, is offline due to record low Danube water levels that prevent the plant's suction nozzles from reaching water needed for cooling.
bottom_line: The timing of Paks's shutdown, coinciding with peak summer electricity demand and extreme heat, forces Hungary into emergency conservation measures while the broader Danube region grapples with simultaneous water and energy crises. Climatologists forecast no relief until mid-September; if water levels do not recover by then, the question shifts from temporary emergency protocols to sustained structural constraints on European energy supply.
body: Hungary's Paks nuclear power plant is shutting down entirely for the first time, unable to draw cooling water from the Danube River as water levels hit record lows, according to BBC reporting. The closure threatens to deepen an energy crisis across Central Europe at the moment when demand peaks during an extreme heat event.

Prime Minister Peter Magyar warned that Hungary's energy supply could become critical from Monday onward due to the Paks shutdown. Temperatures are expected to hover around 37 degrees Celsius for a week. In response, Magyar asked Hungarians to limit electricity consumption between 17:00 and 22:00, including refraining from charging electric cars and using air conditioning during peak hours. The government said a "rotational shutdown regime" was possible if other conservation measures proved insufficient, under which it would compile a list of major electricity and water consumers whose consumption could be limited.

The Danube's collapse is regional, not localized. According to Romania's National Institute of Hydrology, the average river flow where the Danube enters the country is 4,700 cubic metres per second in July. On Wednesday, it measured less than one-third of that, at 1,600 cubic metres per second, with forecasts showing further decline to 1,500 cubic metres per second by Tuesday. Serbia's hydrologist Dejan Vladikovic said the Danube had fallen to levels not seen for 50 to 60 years, a decline he attributed not only to current high temperatures but also to low rainfall during spring.

The water crisis extends across critical infrastructure. In Romania, one of the two nuclear reactors at the Cernavoda power plant, which supplies about 20 percent of the country's electricity, was shut down. The state was attempting to avoid closing the second 706-megawatt reactor on Thursday. Shipping has ground to a halt in Bulgaria. Border police evacuated 186 passengers from the Viking Ullur river cruise ship after it ran aground near Vidin earlier in the week; passengers had been running low on food and water because the vessel could not dock. Ivan Zhekov, head of river supervision at Bulgaria's maritime administration agency, said, "I have never heard of such low levels over the years. There has certainly not been a similar situation since 1990."

The Danube runs 2,857 kilometers through 19 countries. Europe is heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service. Climatologists did not expect improvement on the Danube until mid-September. In Serbia, temperatures are forecast to climb as high as 38 degrees Celsius on Friday, locally reaching 40 degrees Celsius, with night-time temperatures in Belgrade as high as 26 degrees Celsius. Meanwhile, vast areas of France and Spain have experienced some of the most intense and widespread wildfires in living memory, leading to hundreds of thousands of evacuations.
